doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Listening to the whole band and learning the vocabulary
summary: Berroa says players must learn the vocabulary of each style, not rules.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You said, this is a great story, and it reminds me a bit of the video that you did, one of your early videos and you were addressing a question about listening to the Latin rhythms and trying to figure them out, and your response was, “You must listen to the whole band to make sense of what’s going on.”
So I would guess that that was a practice of yours, listening to the whole band, including Dizzy if it was a Dizzy record, which served you well.

Yup. Yup. You have to listen to everything. That’s one of the things that is going to link you to success, learning the genre. For many years I have seen a lot of people, and especially, but it also happens with jazz. A lot of the young musicians, they just concentrate on their instrument. They just concentrate about getting, playing the right

scales, the right intervals, the embouchure or whatever or the instrument technique and they don’t care about the vocabulary. How? Why is this happening? What the drummer is doing. Why the bass player — you have to learn how to comp, on the drums because some people, some musicians who in my opinion can not play several types of music, they call that “the rules.” There are no rules, it is vocabulary. It’s something that you need to learn, and even you can expand the vocabulary, take the vocabulary to a different level, but there is a foundation that in my opinion if you know that foundation, if you study, if you learn that it’s going to allow you to take that music to a different level. It is the vocabulary. And it’s the vocabulary that you need to learn. And that vocabulary cannot be taught with this accent that I’m talking to you now, the accent, that my English has. That vocabulary, you have to find the right accent and you have to do your homework. You have to do it. Because when you’re going to play that music it’s the same thing that I have always been talking about, the so-called Latin music, you need to learn that. [gap] self respect that you know, that [gap] has evolved out of music or genres. I don’t know how it’s correct, genre or style of music. So forgive me. That’s something that you have to dedicate your time and learn. It’s not like okay you learn two patterns, two Afro-Cuban or what everybody call “two Latin patterns” and you are an expert and you can play that music. It’s not like that. There is something to be learned. So that’s my opinion. And that’s something that I have been saying for years. It is a vocabulary, bebop, that is a vocabulary. Rock. It is a vocabulary. Cha-cha-cha, a rumba, samba, bossa nova, — those genres, there is a vocabulary that you need to learn if you really want to play that and to be effective.
